The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo

EXOR N.V. (EXO-NL): a sound claim on Ferrari, compounding NAV at about 7% a year, at a near-record 56% discount that only a dated decision in March 2027 is likely to narrow

For Richard. 26 November 2026. Share price €71.6 on 19 November 2026. Money in euros; "m" is millions, "bn" billions.

Three terms used throughout. NAV is net asset value: the market value of EXOR's holdings and cash, less its debt. The discount is how far EXOR's share price sits below NAV per share. Net cash earnings are dividends and interest received, less head-office costs, interest paid and tax, leaving out changes in the market value of the holdings. Net cash earnings are the basis of the brokers' EPS and of the model's forecasts.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

At today's price, an EXOR share costs little more than its slice of the Ferrari stake. EXOR is the Agnelli family's listed holding company. It owns large minority stakes in Ferrari, Philips, CNH and Stellantis, a healthcare cluster, funds run by its own manager (Lingotto), and cash from two years of disposals. NAV was €32.0bn at 30 June 2026 (€157.90 a share). EXOR's market value is about €14.3bn, a discount to NAV of about 56%, close to the widest on record. The Ferrari stake alone is worth about €61 per EXOR share at June marks (about €68 today, on my estimate), against a share price of about €72. The share price therefore assigns almost no value to the rest of EXOR's NAV.

The case in five conclusions

1
EXOR's forecastable earnings are not what drives its share price. Net cash earnings are mechanical: about 85% to 90% of 2027's will have been declared by early March 2027. But net cash earnings are only about 1% of NAV. EXOR's share price equals NAV per share times one minus the discount, and those two terms are set by Ferrari's share price, by the market's view of the discount and by one board decision.
2
The base case delivers an equity-like return and no more. NAV per share grows about 7% a year: about 5 points from the holdings' share prices, 1 to 2.5 points from buying back EXOR shares at less than half of NAV, and under 1 point from retained earnings. At an unchanged discount, the total return is about 9% to December 2027 and about 22% to June 2029 (about 8% a year).
3
The upside rests on one decision with a date. After pending disposals close and the current buyback ends, EXOR will hold about €3.2bn of cash: 22% of its market value and half the value of the shares held outside the family. Management has said it will update on the use of that cash with the FY2026 results in late March 2027. A capital return of €2bn or more (about a one-in-eight chance) would add 8% to 9% to NAV per share and about 10% to FY2028 EPS. A return of that size is the only credible route to a narrower discount.
4
The downside is driven by markets and amplified by the discount, but it is not permanent. Ferrari is about 40% of NAV and trades on a premium multiple. In both recent drawdowns, EXOR's share price fell about twice as far as its NAV per share. A stress case costs 15% to 23%. EXOR has no refinancing or forced-selling risk.
5
The brokers' expectations are too high, not too low. EXOR gives no guidance to beat. The model's EPS is a little above the three forecasting brokers' for 2027 and below theirs for 2028. All six covering brokers rate the shares Buy, with a median target of €110 that assumes the discount narrows to about a third. The likelier surprise is the brokers cutting their targets, not EXOR's numbers rising.

Against your test (outcomes and upgrade odds unusually skewed to the positive), EXOR does not qualify today. The probability-weighted share price at end-2027 is about €76 to €77, slightly below the base case, because the downside case (about 23% likely) is more probable than the two upside cases combined (about 20%), even though the downside move is smaller. EXOR becomes a setup on either of two observable events: a capital return large enough to matter to outside holders, or NAV per share starting to beat the index.

Four judgements move the shares most (arithmetic in #9): whether the discount stays near 56%; Ferrari's share price; how EXOR uses its cash in March 2027; and when Stellantis resumes paying a dividend.

The model's headline return of minus 77% to December 2027 is a measurement artefact, not a view on the shares. The model applies a P/E range formed on a different earnings basis (#11 and #12).

#1 Operating environment: tailwinds and headwinds

Bottom lineEXOR's external environment is split but, from here, mildly positive for NAV and income. No external catalyst is dated, and the main exposure is Ferrari's valuation, not Ferrari's demand.

Evidence. EXOR's environment is the value-weighted environment of its holdings, plus the market's appetite for holding companies.

Investors are currently risk-off towards holding companies as a group (the median peer fell 2.4% over the three months to October 2026), and holding-company discounts tend to widen in such periods. EXOR does not hedge its currency exposure: a 10% stronger euro against the dollar cuts NAV by about €0.56bn.

  • The industrial headwinds are loud, but they now carry little weight. CNH and Stellantis together are 18% of NAV, and their dividends are already nil (Stellantis) or token (CNH). Because EXOR's Stellantis stake has halved in value, a further 30% fall in Stellantis's shares now costs about 2% of NAV, half what the same fall cost a year ago.
  • Ferrari's tailwind is quiet but concentrated, and Ferrari's risk is its valuation, not its demand. Consensus already puts Ferrari's 2027 EBIT margin at 30.5%, above the company's own 2030 floor.
  • External forces explain why NAV lagged, not most of the discount. The holding-company peer basket explains only about a quarter of EXOR's daily share-price moves, and better-regarded peers re-rated while EXOR de-rated.

So what. From here, external forces are mildly positive for EXOR's income, because the cyclical dividends can only rise from near zero from 2028. They are two-sided for NAV and unhelpful for the discount. No external event offers a dated catalyst in the next six months.

Counter-case. Ferrari's Greater China shipments fell 42% in Q3 2026. Management calls the fall deliberate allocation, and China is under 10% of Ferrari's sales, but it is the first sign of a wealth effect in a franchise priced as immune to one. A weak Chinese home market also pushes more cheap Chinese car exports into Europe just when Stellantis is weakest. And the recent relief for CNH and Stellantis (lower US tariff rates, easier emissions rules) rests on political decisions that can reverse.

What would change my view. Upward: two quarters of falling Stellantis US dealer stock alongside positive industrial cash flow; CNH's 2027 order books confirming a turn. Downward: Ferrari's order book shortening, or resale values of its regular models falling; Ferrari's China weakness spreading to other regions.

Against the market. I agree with the prevailing reading of EXOR as a Ferrari proxy carrying cyclical baggage in an out-of-favour sector. I differ on what the baggage now weighs. The market narrative still treats Stellantis as EXOR's swing factor. At 7% of NAV and with a nil dividend, Stellantis is the swing factor for EXOR's 2028 to 2030 income, but no longer for its NAV.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. Ferrari (38% of NAV) has a strong, order-book-backed tailwind and healthcare (about 17%) a mild improving one, while the loud industrial headwinds (CNH at the trough, Stellantis structurally pressed) now weigh only 18% of NAV with dividends already nil or token, so the income skew from 2028 is mildly positive; against that, a risk-off regime widening holding-company discounts, Ferrari's 42% Greater China drop and reversible tariff relief. I sit above the group's 45 because the headwinds' remaining reach is small: a mild net positive with no dated catalyst, below OEM International's broad recovery and just above Kerry's neutral environment.

#2 Internally-driven corporate change

Bottom lineEXOR's corporate change is real, well funded and positive for NAV per share. But its decisive act, the use of €3.2bn of cash, is undated, and on EXOR's own record buybacks have not narrowed the discount.

Evidence. Three changes are complete and one is open.

Done: Simplification
EXOR has exited GEDI, NUO, Lifenet, Iveco and (closing in the first half of 2027) Welltec, at more than 1.4 times invested capital in aggregate. Welltec is being sold at about 2.4 times cost and in line with its carrying value, which supports EXOR's marks on its other unlisted holdings.
Done: Balance sheet
Loan-to-value is 4.7%, against a self-imposed ceiling of 15%.
Done: Organisation
A deputy chief executive now oversees the holdings so that John Elkann can concentrate on investing. The investment criteria are explicit: tickets of at least €2bn for 15% to 20% stakes with a board seat, in healthcare, luxury or technology.
Open: Use of the cash
A €500m on-market buyback runs to the March 2027 results (€196m completed by 23 November 2026). Beyond the €500m programme, management promises only patience.

Inference.

  • EXOR's transformation has stopped at the point of raising cash. Every step that would turn the cash into per-share value at scale is still undecided.
  • The cash is a one-off stock, but narrowing a discount needs a recurring flow. After the ordinary dividend, recurring income can fund only about €134m of buybacks in 2027, under 1% of EXOR's market value. Any larger buyback must come from the €3.2bn of cash, from debt or from selling assets. The €3.2bn can pay for about two and a half years of buybacks at today's pace, or for one new large stake, but not for both.
  • The form of a capital return matters as much as its size. What counts for the discount is how much cash reaches holders outside the family, relative to the €6.3bn of shares they own. The family took 27% of the 2023 tender and 57% of the 2025 tender. A repeat of the 2025 tender (€1bn, of which the family took €570m) would put about €0.43bn in outside hands. That €0.43bn is less than the current €500m market programme delivers in six months, if the family is not selling into the programme (its participation is not disclosed). The most likely "raise" in March 2027 would therefore not be an escalation for outside holders.
  • Both management and the family gain from a tender. Management's 2026 to 2028 options are struck at €86.46. The base case puts the shares at about €81 to €83 at end-2028, so the options pay out only if the discount narrows to about 53% to 54% or less. The family has used both past tenders to reduce its own debt. These two interests make a further tender more likely than management's "patience" language suggests, without making it larger.
So what. Model EXOR's corporate change as a reliable source of NAV-per-share growth (about 2% from the current programme) and as an unexercised option on the discount.

Counter-case. The same management has a 15-year record of large structural acts and may be under-promising again. Against that, four risks are real. A €2bn stake bought at full price would confirm the discount. A Stellantis capital increase would cost EXOR about €0.8bn as its share of a €5bn raise. EXOR's marks on unlisted holdings are still falling (Institut Mérieux was cut by €276m in six months). And the 23-person head office loses its chief operating officer in January 2027.

What would change my view. Upward: a capital return of €2bn or more; a market buyback renewed at today's pace (about €100m a month) for the whole of 2027; or a stated annual return policy. Downward: a large stake bought at a premium.

Against the market. The brokers' targets and the investor narrative treat the cash and the buyback as catalysts for a re-rating. I treat them as proven sources of NAV-per-share growth but unproven sources of re-rating: about €2.5bn of buybacks since 2021 retired about 14% of EXOR's shares while the discount widened by about 18 points.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. A completed simplification (GEDI, NUO, Lifenet, Iveco, Welltec at over 1.4 times cost, supporting unlisted marks), a 4.7% loan-to-value and a €500m buyback adding about 2% to NAV per share are real and funded, but the decisive act on €3.2bn of cash (22% of market value) is undated, past buybacks did not narrow the discount, unlisted marks are still falling, the COO leaves in January and a full-price stake or Stellantis capital call could absorb the cash. Coherent with the group's 60: a well-resourced, largely repair-and-tidy programme whose earnings effect is modest, just below Odfjell Drilling's accretive acquisition and above Shell's incremental self-help.

#3 Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Bottom lineEXOR's foundations are sound where they protect value (Ferrari, the balance sheet, low costs) and ordinary where they would have to create it (new stakes, the industrial holdings, minority holders' influence). They support NAV growth near the market's rate with a low risk of permanent loss, but they give no reason for the discount to narrow.

Evidence.

  • Holdings. Ferrari sits in a concentrated, margin-first niche with a scarcity model: price and mix added about 11% to revenue in Q3 2026 while shipments fell 1%, the EBIT margin is about 30%, and 84% of cars go to existing owners. bioMérieux is in a two-player market. Philips is third in a rational three-player imaging market and has lost its US sleep-device franchise. CNH is second or third in its markets and is losing technology share to Deere. Stellantis is losing share in a European market where Chinese makers went from almost nothing to 10% to 12% of registrations in six years.
  • Holding company. EXOR has 23 staff, management costs of about 8 basis points of gross assets on its own measure, an A- credit rating and almost no tax. It also holds voting power well above its economic stakes (about 46% of CNH's votes for about 30% of its economics).
  • Management. The incentive plan pays out on NAV per share beating the MSCI World over 2026 to 2028.
  • Governance. The chief executive was paid €14.85m in a year when NAV per share fell 8%.
16.3%
NAV per share a year, 2009 to 2025 (MSCI World 11.6%)
(13.5) / (15.7) pts
behind the index in 2025 and H1 2026
56% / 85%

Inference.

  • EXOR's competitive advantage is borrowed, mostly from Ferrari. The holding company's own strengths (permanent capital, access to deals, low cost) are genuine but give it no pricing power over its own valuation. Weighted by value, the moats are widening for about 40% of NAV and narrowing for about a quarter.
  • EXOR's long-run record came from a different kind of act from the one now planned. The record was built on a few structural moves: the Ferrari spin-off, the Fiat Chrysler and PSA merger, and the PartnerRe sale. The act now planned is a minority stake in a listed company bought at market price, and EXOR's record on such stakes since 2022 is ordinary: Philips has returned about 12% a year on EXOR's own count, Clarivate is down, and venture investing has been abandoned.
  • EXOR's financial profile is a fortress around a small engine. The balance sheet removes the usual holding-company tail risks, but the recurring earnings are too small to fund a meaningful return of capital.
  • Family control is the root of the discount. No outside holder can force EXOR to deliver NAV to shareholders, and the family's revealed preferences (keeping Juventus, staying in Stellantis) are not purely about per-share value. The holding companies that trade near NAV (Investor AB, Industrivärden) combine NAV out-performance with operating control of their holdings and steady cash returns.
Counter-case: bull
EXOR combines one of Europe's best franchises with an almost debt-free balance sheet, run at almost no cost by an owner whose own wealth is in the shares.
Counter-case: bear
The one large holding the chief executive chaired directly (Stellantis) lost €22.3bn in 2025, and the incentive plan's goal is already far behind: I put the chance of NAV per share beating the index over 2026 to 2028 at about one in five.

What would change my view. A new stake that visibly earns EXOR's "double-digit" return hurdle; a plan for Stellantis; steps that give outside holders more of the cash.

Against the market. I agree with the common view of EXOR as "Ferrari and friends at half price", with the quality concentrated in Ferrari. I add one qualification the narrative omits: EXOR's "strong capital-allocation record" describes structural acts that are no longer on the agenda.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. One fortress unit (Ferrari, about 40% of NAV, scarcity pricing, 30% EBIT margin) plus bioMérieux's duopoly and a 23-person, 8bp-cost, A- rated holding sit beside Philips' middling position, CNH and Stellantis losing share, an ordinary record on new minority stakes since 2022 (Philips about 12% a year, Clarivate down) and a family control structure that gives outside holders no voice; the reported ROIC of (9.7)% (2.7th percentile) and (455)% operating margin are fair-value and perimeter artefacts and tell nothing. Coherent with groups of 52 to 58: the level's 'one fortress unit beside ordinary ones', above Shell, below Helios Towers' proven incremental returns.

#4 Guidance, expectations management and track record

Bottom lineEXOR's commitments are as conservative as commitments can be, and it has always met them. But EXOR gives no earnings guidance to raise, and its record on capital returns stops at €1bn, below what the brokers' targets need.

Evidence.

  • EXOR gives no earnings guidance. Its only commitments are policy limits, all far inside actual levels and met every year on record (table below).
  • EXOR's tone is deliberately low. Management speaks of "another difficult year" and promises to "remain very disciplined", and it cut the loan-to-value ceiling from 20% to 15%.
  • EXOR's real "guidance" is the size of its capital returns, and that record has a ceiling. EXOR launched a buyback at four of its last nine results dates; the largest was €1bn. It has returned a sixth to a third of its disposal proceeds, in blocks of €0.5bn to €1bn. The dividend rose from €0.44 to €0.46 to €0.49 and has been held at €0.49.
  • The habit of beating and raising guidance lives one level down, in the holdings. Ferrari raised its 2026 guidance twice; Philips beat its 2025 margin guidance; CNH moves with its cycle; Stellantis misses (its Q3 2026 industrial cash outflow was about €4bn, against about €2.65bn expected).
  • The sell-side's record on EXOR's income is poor. The consensus FY2027 EPS estimate fell 76% in twelve months, as brokers moved to the investment-entity basis and lost the Stellantis dividend.

Inference. The dynamic you look for (conservative guidance, delivered, then raised, with estimates following) does not exist at EXOR. At EXOR the roles are reversed:

The company: the conservative party
Low tone, policy limits far inside actual levels, no earnings guidance to raise or cut.
The sell-side: the optimistic party
Target prices that assume the discount shrinks; FY2027 EPS already rebased down 76% in a year.

Ferrari's and Philips' upgrades reach EXOR as higher NAV, not as higher EPS.

So what. There is no guidance cut to fear and no guidance raise to wait for. EXOR's one discretionary announcement, the March 2027 capital return, has a most likely size, on the record, that does not move the discount.

Counter-case. Management under-promises on capital too. Its tone is cautious, but its actions have been opportunistic: it sold 4% of Ferrari near the highs and tendered for €1bn of its own shares at a 50% discount. A positive surprise in March 2027 would be in character.

What would change my view. A stated return policy (a percentage of NAV or of market value each year), which would turn a discretionary act into something estimates could anchor on.

Against the market. I agree that EXOR offers nothing to model against. I differ from the brokers on what the record implies for March 2027: the brokers' targets price a narrower discount, while the record points to a return of €0.5bn to €1bn.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. EXOR gives no earnings guidance (neutral) and every policy limit it does guide on (loan-to-value at most 15%, now cut from 20%; free cash flow covering the dividend 5.9 times; costs under 10bp) is met every year with a deliberately low tone, which the levels place above 50; held near it because its own stretching goal (NAV per share beating the index, the incentive plan's test) has been missed by 13.5 and 15.7 points in 2025 and H1 2026, and capital returns have a €1bn ceiling. Slightly above the groups' 46 to 50 because conservative, always-met self-set limits count; between CVS Group's met targets and Sdiptech's untested ones.

#5 Pricing power, leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Bottom lineEXOR has genuine operating leverage and one powerful price of its own, the price at which it buys back its shares. Both act on NAV per share and on a small earnings line. The gearing that reaches the share price is the discount: each point is worth about 2.3% on the price.

Evidence and inference, by mechanism.

  • Operating leverage is real but small. Head-office costs and interest are fixed at about €150m a year, so net cash earnings move about 1.3 to 1.5 times as fast as dividend income. The resulting profit growth from the 2027 trough to 2030 is outsized (figures above), but it is growth on a line worth about 1% of NAV.
  • The dividend stream falls fast and recovers slowly. The cyclical holdings cut dividends to zero within a year of trouble and restore them only after a full year of positive cash flow. This lag is why EXOR's income troughs in 2027, a year after the holdings' own earnings.
  • Financial leverage is light on value but heavy on income. EXOR's debt is trivial against its assets, but the interest on that debt takes about a third of 2027 net cash earnings. The cash EXOR holds alongside the debt earns less than the debt costs, a drag of about €30m to €40m a year.
  • Pricing power is borrowed, except for one price EXOR sets itself. Ferrari's pricing power is among the best demonstrated in listed equities. The one price EXOR sets is the price at which it buys back its own shares: each euro spent at today's discount buys about €2.25 of NAV.
  • There is no cost scope at the holding company. EXOR's costs are already at the floor for the sector. The holdings' own cost programmes (Stellantis, Philips, CNH) are heavily offset by inflation and reinvestment, and they reach EXOR's income late, mostly from 2029.

Feedback loops.

Reinforcing, positive
Ferrari's scarcity loop; buybacks, which become more accretive as the discount widens.
Reinforcing, negative
Stellantis's loop of excess inventory and rising incentives, still running.
Balancing, holding the discount
Income too small to fund a recurring flow of buybacks; market buybacks that shrink the free float; and a discount that widens when NAV falls.
So what. The gearing in the earnings model does not reach the share price through EPS. The gearing that does reach it is the discount. That gearing has worked against holders on the way down and has not yet worked for them on the way up.

Counter-case. The loops could flip together. A break in Stellantis's inventory loop combined with a large return of capital would turn both the income recovery and the discount into reinforcing positives. Either change alone has not been enough.

What would change my view. Evidence that buybacks sustained above about 5% of market value a year narrow EXOR's discount; a break in Stellantis's inventory loop.

Against the market. No broker builds a case on EXOR's operating leverage, and I agree. I differ from the narrative that treats buybacks as leverage on the discount: the accretion arithmetic of buybacks is certain, but the re-rating is not.

Score: 47, set by the Rater. Fixed head-office and interest costs of about €150m make net cash earnings move 1.3 to 1.5 times dividend income (EPS +88% on revenue +63% from 2027 to 2030, below the Universe's typical two times), there is no cost-out scope, interest takes a third of 2027 earnings, and the cyclical dividend stream is asymmetric (cut within a year, restored late). Pricing power is borrowed from Ferrari and the one price EXOR sets, buying back shares at €2.25 of NAV per euro, is a real accretive loop, so this is the level's moderate gearing with no strong gear, slightly below the ordinary mix; coherent with the groups' 52 and 33.

#6 Forecast financials

Bottom lineThe forecasts show a dated income trough in 2027 and a double-digit recovery from it, on a line worth about 1% of NAV. Meanwhile NAV per share compounds at a market-like 7% a year, slower than EXOR's past.

What the numbers say.

  • 2027 is the trough in EXOR's income. Revenue falls 55% because the Iveco one-off and Lingotto's 2025 performance distribution drop out, exited holdings stop paying, and Stellantis pays nothing.
  • EXOR's income has changed character. In 2024 Stellantis supplied about 69% of EXOR's dividends; in 2027 Ferrari and Philips supply about 75%. The dividend stream is steadier and about 60% smaller.
  • The EPS recovery is double-digit, but from a low base and on the less reliable dividends. EPS grows about 23% a year from 2027 to 2030. More than half of the revenue increase comes from Stellantis and CNH, and only about a third from Ferrari and Philips. Even in 2030, EPS stays below the roughly €4.2 of 2024.
  • NAV per share grows about 7% a year, the same pace as from end-2022 to mid-2026 and less than half the long-run record. On neither earnings nor NAV are the next four years better than the past.
  • The balance sheet re-gears by choice. The base case buys about €0.6bn more of Philips in 2027 and a new €2bn stake in 2028, part-funded by about €1bn of debt. Cash falls from about €2.9bn to about €0.5bn, loan-to-value rises to about 10%, and interest paid rises from €98m to about €150m. A stake bought at market price is roughly neutral for both earnings and NAV at the time of purchase.

What would change my view. Stellantis's February 2027 cash-flow guidance; the Lingotto mark in March 2027; the timing and funding of a new stake.

Against the market. On income I am close to the brokers. Against the three brokers who forecast it, the model's FY2027 EPS is above both their median (€1.28) and their mean (€1.50), and its FY2028 EPS is below both (€1.81 and €2.00). On NAV I am above the brokers: their book value per share grows 2% to 3% a year, against my 7%.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. The reported base is inflated by the one-off Iveco dividend, so the clean base is the honest one and gives C; the consensus 28% next-year growth (89.7th percentile) only measures the rebound from the 2027 trough. Placed low in the band because about two points a year are buybacks, more than half the revenue recovery rests on cyclical Stellantis and CNH dividends, 2030 EPS stays below 2024's €4.2 and NAV per share (7%) compounds slower than EXOR's past.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative

Bottom lineThe scope for upgrades is confined to NAV marks and to one low-probability capital decision. The estimates that matter most, the brokers' target prices, are more likely to come down than to go up.

Evidence: what can move in the next 6 to 12 months, and in which direction.

ItemLikely directionOdds
EXOR policy limitsMetNear certain
March 2027 capital returnAbout €0.5bn renewed 45%; about €1bn tender 30%; €2bn or more 10% to 12%; none, or cash committed to a stake, 15% As shown
FY2027 EPS (three brokers)Small upgrades as dividends are declaredHigher 45%, lower 20%
FY2028 EPS (three brokers)Cut as the Stellantis dividend slipsLower 55% to 60%
Brokers' NAV estimatesUp mechanically in any ordinary market yearHigher 55%
Target prices (median €110)More likely cut than raisedLower 40%, higher 30%
Ratings (six Buys)Can only falln/a
Ferrari's first 2027 guidance (February)Below a full consensus, then raised during the yearBelow 60%; raised later 70%

Inference.

  • Estimates will move, but on numbers that do not move the shares. Upgrades to FY2027 EPS are likely and irrelevant to the share price. Where upgrades would matter (target prices, which embed the discount), the likely direction is down.
  • The market narrative already contains the bull case. Brokers, specialist discount investors and retail commentary all cite the record discount, the cash, the accretive buyback and the March 2027 decision. The investors who buy discounted holding companies already own EXOR. What my work adds to the narrative is mostly cautious: the limit that income places on buybacks, the family's share of tenders, and the one-off nature of Lingotto's 2025 distribution.
  • Three modest positives are missing from the narrative. EXOR's cash is half the value of the outside holders' shares; management's option strike price sits just above the base-case share-price path; and the 2027 income trough is already in every model, so EXOR's income line holds no negative surprise for a year.
  • The risk comes before the option. Ferrari's first 2027 guidance and Stellantis's cash guidance arrive in February 2027; the capital decision arrives in late March. A soft February would lower NAV and probably widen the discount just ahead of the decision. A wider discount would make any tender more accretive and, on management's past behaviour, more likely.
So what. Upgrade scope of the kind you look for is absent. The case for the next 12 months rests on one announcement and on market marks.

Counter-case. Flat markets, clean Ferrari guidance and a €1bn tender could together read as "delivery" and lift target prices. But the brokers' targets already assume that outcome, so the marginal buyer would need a new reason.

What would change my view. The March 2027 announcement itself: a return of €2bn or more, or a tender in which outside holders receive most of the cash, would open a favourable gap against my base case.

Against the market. I am in line with the brokers on 2027 income, below them on 2028, above them on NAV, and far more cautious than them on the discount. My view is closer to the share price's own verdict than to the brokers'.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. The de facto guidance line, the March 2027 capital return, most likely brings €0.5bn to €1bn (75%), which on the record does not escalate cash to outside holders, against 10% to 12% odds of €2bn or more; FY2027 EPS is more likely raised (45% against 20%) but FY2028 more likely cut (55% to 60%), target prices lean down and six Buys can only fall, while the narrative already holds the bull case. Upside is confined to NAV marks and a low-probability decision, so a little above the group's 38, below Tele2's small raises and level with IMCD's limited scope.

#8 Current momentum

Bottom lineMomentum is absent in guidance, estimates and narrative, and tentative in the share price. EXOR is a stock that has stopped falling but has not started a trend.

Evidence.

  • Sell-side. The revision-momentum score is 1 (neutral). Target prices are down 3% over both three and six months. The share of Buy ratings is 86%, down 14 points over six months. The 26% one-month rise in consensus FY2027 EPS is noise: it comes from three brokers using three different definitions of earnings.
  • Technical. Technical momentum is rated C. The share price is 3.6% above its 200-day moving average, which has risen in only one of the last twelve months. Relative strength is at the 45th percentile. The share price returned plus 0.4% over three months, plus 7.5% over six and plus 1.6% over twelve, against a sector median of about plus 12% over twelve months (my calculation from the peer table).
  • Peers. Peer momentum is mixed, and unhelpful where it matters. The better-regarded holding companies have momentum (Investor AB and Sofina rated B; Georgia Capital A). EXOR's closest comparators do not (Peugeot Invest and Prosus F; GBL D).
  • Holdings. Ferrari's brokers have been raising targets since its Q3 2026 beat; Stellantis's brokers have been cutting.
  • Other ratings. Thematic Fit/Momentum is rated C. The valuation rating is F, an artefact of the change in earnings basis (#11).

Inference. There is no momentum in guidance, estimates or narrative. The share price has stopped falling and has beaten a flat peer basket by about 6 points over six months. That six-month period coincides both with EXOR's buyback (roughly a tenth of daily trading) and with Ferrari's recovery, and I cannot separate the two effects. The overlap is itself informative: the first real test of the share price comes when the buyback programme ends in March 2027.

So what. Momentum neither supports nor undermines the case; it confirms a stock at rest.

Counter-case. A stock that outperforms its peers while its estimates are flat and its narrative unchanged may be showing the first effect of a buyback that is large relative to its free float.

What would change my view. A rising 200-day average for several months; relative strength above the 60th percentile without help from Ferrari; a first target-price increase from a covering broker.

Against the market. I agree with the dashboard's readings. I would not read the recent rise in EPS estimates as momentum.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. Both measures are negative but neither is in the bottom fifth, so D; the +19% three-month EPS revision (95th percentile) is basis noise from three brokers, target prices are down 3%, the Buy share fell 14 points, guidance is absent (not negative) and the narrative is unchanged. Placed high in the band because the price has stopped falling, sits 3.6% above a flat 200-day average and beat a flat peer basket by about 6 points over six months under the buyback, while comparable peers are mixed.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Bottom lineEXOR's case is simple to track and carries a low risk of permanent loss, but its return is hard to predict. The return hangs on Ferrari's share price, on a discount that has widened in every drawdown, and on one board decision.

The case is easy to follow but hard to predict. Four holdings priced daily make up about 70% of gross assets; EXOR reports its buyback weekly; US car inventory is published monthly; and three events are dated. The case is hard to predict because its drivers are market prices and a discretionary decision, and there are too few of them to average out.

Three ranges of outcome, not one.

Scenarios to end-2027.

ScenarioOddsWhat happensDiscountShare price
Baseabout 57%NAV per share up about 7% a year; buybacks of €0.5bn to €1bn a year, possibly as a €1bn tender53% to 57%€73 to €82
Large capital returnabout 12%€2bn or more returned from March 202747% to 50%€92 to €100
Favourable marketsabout 8%Ferrari moves towards brokers' targets; CNH turns; Stellantis stabilisesabout 50% to 52%€88 to €95
Stressabout 23%Ferrari falls about 25%, or markets turn risk-off; possibly a Stellantis capital call58% to 60%€55 to €61

Weighted by their odds, the four scenarios give an end-2027 share price of about €76 to €77.

The four judgements that move the shares, and the arithmetic if each one is wrong

1. The discount stays at about 56%.

  • Step 1: end-2027 NAV per share of about €175 times 0.44 gives a share price of about €77.
  • Step 2: at a 51% discount, €175 times 0.49 is about €86 (plus 11%); at a 61% discount, €175 times 0.39 is about €68 (minus 11%).
  • Step 3: total earnings and NAV do not change. The 2027 buyback of €625m retires about 8.1m shares at €77 but about 9.2m at €68, so a wider discount adds about 0.6% to EPS and NAV per share, and a narrower one subtracts about 0.5%.
  • Reading: the discount moves the share price by about 11% per five points, and moves per-share fundamentals by about half a percent in the opposite direction.

2. Ferrari's share price holds.

  • Step 1: EXOR owns 37.77m Ferrari shares, worth about €13.6bn today on my estimate, or about €68 per EXOR share.
  • Step 2: a 25% fall in Ferrari's shares removes €3.4bn, or about €17 per EXOR share. NAV per share falls about 10%, from about €164 to about €147.
  • Step 3: at an unchanged discount, EXOR's shares fall 10% to about €64. On the pattern of 2025 and the first half of 2026 (share price down about twice as far as NAV), they fall about 20% to about €57.
  • Step 4: EXOR's earnings barely move. If the cause were Ferrari's price and mix growth halving in 2027, Ferrari's earnings would grow about 5% instead of 10%, EXOR's 2028 Ferrari dividend would be about €157m instead of €165m, FY2028 net income about €320m instead of €328m, and EPS €1.69 instead of €1.73.
  • Reading: Ferrari is a NAV judgement of high sensitivity and an earnings judgement of almost none. A 15% rise in Ferrari's shares adds about €10 a share to NAV (6%).

3. March 2027 brings €0.5bn to €1bn, not €2bn or more. If instead EXOR tenders for €2bn at about €75 a share and defers the new stake:

  • Step 1: the tender retires about 26.7m shares. The average FY2028 share count falls from about 190m to about 167.5m (minus 12%).
  • Step 2: FY2028 revenue falls from €509m to about €481m (about €9m less interest on cash; about €19m less Philips dividend without the larger Philips stake).
  • Step 3: interest paid falls from €125m to about €108m because no new debt is raised. Net income is about €318m against €328m (minus 3%).
  • Step 4: EPS is about €1.90 against €1.73 (plus 10%). NAV per share rises 8% to 9% at once (about €32.5bn less €2bn, over about 169m shares instead of 196m).
  • Step 5: the shares rise 8% to 9% with no change in the discount, and about 23% if the discount narrows to 50%.
  • Reading: the decision is close to neutral for total earnings and decisive for per-share value. The reverse error, a €2bn stake bought at full price in 2027, costs about €0.10 of 2027 EPS in lost interest, leaves NAV unchanged and closes off the upside scenario.

4. Stellantis pays again from 2029 (nil in 2028, €55m in 2029, €110m in 2030).

  • Later: no Stellantis dividend to 2030 takes FY2029 net income from €441m to about €387m and EPS from €2.37 to about €2.08 (minus 12%), and FY2030 net income from €543m to about €434m and EPS from €2.99 to about €2.39 (minus 20%).
  • Earlier: a dividend of €0.10 a share in 2028 adds about €45m, taking FY2028 EPS from €1.73 to about €1.97 (plus 14%).
  • NAV: a 30% move in Stellantis's shares is about €0.67bn, or €3.4 per EXOR share (2%).
  • A capital call: EXOR's share of a €5bn raise is about €0.8bn of cash out, about €16m a year of lost interest (€0.08 of EPS), and a quarter of the deployable cash gone.

Sector precedents.

  • A record discount has not been a floor. EXOR's discount went from 40% (2020) to 44% (2022) to 51% (May 2025) to 57.6% (June 2026); each extreme was followed by a wider one. Prosus traded for years below the value of its Tencent stake alone, and Peugeot Invest trades at a discount of about 61%.
  • Buybacks alone have a poor record of closing discounts. Wendel bought back 9% of its capital in 2026, and its discount is still near 50%. The cases that worked needed far larger scale or a strong rise in NAV at the same time: Prosus retired about a third of its free float over four years, and Georgia Capital cancelled 11.6% of its shares in a year alongside a 61% rise in NAV per share.
  • NAV growth does most of the work. One broker study attributes about 85% of holding-company returns over five years or more to NAV growth and about 15% to changes in the discount.
  • EXOR gives no shelter in a sell-off. In market-wide shocks, its correlation with peers rises to about 0.75 and its beta is above 1.

Sudden risks. Ferrari fell 16% to 19% in a day when it set its targets in October 2025, and Stellantis fell 18.5% on its preliminary 2025 results. Falls of that kind reach EXOR's NAV the same day. The fat-tail risks are in governance: the litigation over the family's top holding company (low probability, since loyalty voting protects control) and the family's own undisclosed debt.

What limits the damage. No debt matures before 2028; the cash does not fall with markets; and buybacks become more accretive as the discount widens (about €2.50 of NAV per euro at a 60% discount).
So what. Judge EXOR on its range of outcomes, not on a point estimate: roughly minus 20% to plus 35% over 13 months, around a high-single-digit central return, with the odds tilted slightly down and the balance sheet ruling out anything worse than a market loss.

Counter-case. The margin-of-safety reading holds that the share price leaves almost nothing for the holdings other than Ferrari, so bad news outside Ferrari cannot hurt much and any good news is free. The record does not support that reading. A record discount has been a level from which EXOR's discount widened further, and falls caused by Stellantis and the unlisted holdings were amplified in the share price, just as a fall in Ferrari would be.

What would change my view. A drawdown in NAV in which the discount does not widen would be the first evidence of a floor.

Against the market. The market narrative holds the margin-of-safety reading; I do not. I agree with the narrative that the case is simple and carries no balance-sheet risk.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. The case is simple to track (four daily-priced holdings at about 70% of gross assets, weekly buyback data, three dated events) and the balance sheet rules out refinancing or forced selling, but the FY2027 EPS cone is about (12)% to +23% and, more important, the share price hangs on Ferrari's premium multiple, a discount that has widened in every drawdown with price falling twice as far as NAV, a beta above 1 in shocks and one discretionary board decision, a cone of about (20)% to +35% tilted down. Slightly above the group's 42 because there is no leverage, below IMCD's simple model and above Rexel's less trackable earnings.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Bottom line. EXOR is bottoming, with a first tentative turn in the share price and none yet in fundamentals. This reading agrees with the dashboard's starting phase. EXOR turns up only if March 2027 supplies a mechanism or NAV per share starts to beat the index.

Evidence. EXOR is bottoming in three senses, each with its own timing.

Income: a dated trough
2027 is the low point, and it is in every model. Estimates were rebased down by 76% and have stopped falling.
Relative NAV: not yet turned
NAV per share has trailed the index for two and a half years. The holding that caused most of the lag (Stellantis) has halved in value, so its power to hurt has halved too, but nothing yet shows NAV beating the index.
The discount and the price: stopped widening, under a buyback
The discount has eased from 57.6% in June 2026 to about 56% on my estimate. The technical readings in #8 describe a base, not a trend.

So what. A bottoming stock deserves a multiple at the low end of its range (#11) and a wide range of outcomes (#9). The turn has clear, observable triggers, which makes EXOR a case to monitor closely rather than one to forecast.

What would move EXOR to "turning up". Any one of: a capital return that passes the size test in March 2027; NAV per share beating the index over a half-year (visible in the September 2027 results, and daily before them); a break in Stellantis's inventory loop.
What would send EXOR back down. A de-rating of Ferrari after its February 2027 guidance; a Stellantis capital call; a large stake bought at a premium.

Counter-case. The shares have been called a bargain at each of the last four record discounts. The difference now is that the cash and the incentives are in place; the similarity is that the decision to use them is not.

Against the market. The brokers' targets describe a stock already turning up. The share price describes a stock bottoming. I side with the share price.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. The memo's Bottoming is right: the income trough is dated in 2027 and estimates have stopped falling, the discount has eased only from 57.6% to about 56% under a buyback, and NAV per share has yet to beat the index, with no turn in fundamentals and a record that each discount extreme was followed by a wider one. The triggers are clear and dated (March 2027), but until one fires this sits just below Solid State's bottoming-to-turning and level with Linea Directa's bottoming without improvement in forecasts.

#11 The fair multiple

Bottom lineThe guideline's 6.51 times earnings is the right rule applied to a broken series. On price to NAV, the fair multiple for a bottoming EXOR is about 0.43 to 0.48 times, roughly where the shares trade today (0.44 times).

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple is 6.51 times two-year-forward earnings: the 30th percentile of the stock's own history, which is the setting for a Bottoming stock. The multiple today is 36.1 times on consensus earnings (42.7 times on the model's own). The dashboard's valuation rating is F, with the P/E at the 100th percentile of its own ten-year history.

My view: the guideline's rule is sound, but the earnings series it is applied to is broken.
August 2022 to January 2025: old basis
5 to 11 times
Shares €59 to €101; implied forward EPS about €8 to €15
From February 2025: net cash earnings
22 to 58 times
Implied forward EPS about €1.3 to €3.8; "earnings" down about 85%, price down about a quarter
  • The denominator changed, not the valuation. The share price fell about a quarter between the two periods, but the "earnings" fell about 85%, because brokers moved from fair-value and consolidated earnings to net cash earnings.
  • The 30th percentile sits entirely in the old earnings basis. Thirty of the 51 months of history are on the old basis, and the 6.51 times comes from those months.
  • Applied to the new earnings, 6.51 times gives a price no seller would accept. 6.51 times about €2.4 of forward EPS is about €15.5 a share, roughly a quarter of the value of the Ferrari stake alone.
  • The F rating and the 100th percentile are the same artefact. Net cash earnings capture only about one sixth of the value EXOR creates in a normal year: about €1.60 to €2.40 a share, against NAV growth of about €11 to €12.

The multiple that carries information is price to NAV. Today it is about 0.44 times (a 56% discount).

  • The guideline's rule, applied to price to NAV. From the data points I hold (a discount of about 40% in 2020, 44% in 2022, 51% in May 2025 and 56% to 58% since; a five-year average of about 46%; about 35% since listing), the 30th percentile of price to NAV over ten years is probably about 0.50 to 0.54 times. That figure is my estimate from scattered points, not a computed percentile.
  • Why I sit a little below that guideline equivalent. The discount has trended one way for five years, so a percentile of that history is a memory of better conditions, not a level to revert to. And at least two-thirds of the discount is specific to EXOR (Stellantis, idle cash, family control), so it will change only for a reason specific to EXOR.
So what. On the right measure, EXOR's shares are about fairly valued for their phase. Each step up the ladder is worth about 11% on the share price per five points of discount.
Counter-case: bull
The since-listing average discount is 35%, and the brokers assume about a third. If any mechanism appears, the ladder is steep.
Counter-case: bear
Peugeot Invest at a 61% discount shows that the range of possible discounts has not been exhausted.

What would change my view. The triggers in #10; a computed ten-year percentile materially different from my estimate.

Against the market. The brokers' fair multiple is about 0.65 times NAV; the market's is 0.44; mine for this phase is 0.43 to 0.48. I agree with the market. I disagree with the brokers on timing, not on where the multiple could go once a mechanism exists.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. The raw readings do not tell the truth: the earnings basis fell about 85% in February 2025 while the price fell a quarter, so the ten-year range and cohort average sit on a different kind of earnings, and 6.51 times would value EXOR at a quarter of its Ferrari stake. On price to NAV the shares are cheap against their own history, but much of that cheapness is deserved for a bottoming, family-controlled holding whose discount has trended wider for five years (the memo's fair 0.43 to 0.48 times brackets today's 0.44), so I move the letter to C, near its middle.

What drives the model's figure.

  • The multiple: the artefact. The whole loss comes from the P/E falling from 42.7 to 6.51 times. For the reasons in #11, that step compares net cash earnings with a P/E range formed on a different kind of earnings. It is not a forecast of the share price.

Reading the table.

  • The return is the NAV growth. Of the roughly 8 points of NAV-per-share growth to end-2027, about 5 come from the holdings' share prices, about 2 from buyback accretion and under 1 from retained earnings.
  • The level of the discount does not set the return; a change in the discount does. At a stable discount, a holder earns NAV growth plus the dividend. Counter-case: downside
The stress case in #9 gives about minus 20%. Neither the upside nor the downside case needs any change to the earnings forecast.

What would change my view. On the base return, the holdings' assumed share-price return of about 5% a year: each point more or less is about a point of total return. On the multiple, the triggers in #10.

Against the market. The brokers' targets imply a return of about plus 50%, almost all of it from a narrower discount. The share price implies an equity-like return from NAV growth. I side with the share price in the base case and value a narrower discount as an option.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. The informative return is NAV-per-share growth of about 7% a year plus a 0.7% dividend at an unchanged discount, with the scenarios weighting slightly below the base; the three-year check of about 22% to June 2029 (about 8% a year) confirms an equity-like return. Placed below the 9% to 10% point (about 48) because the lower tail is larger in probability (23% stress at (15)% to (23)%) than the upper (20%), and the shares fall about twice as far as NAV in drawdowns.

#13 Summary conclusion

EXOR today is a well-run, almost debt-free claim on Ferrari and a handful of other holdings, priced at 44 cents per euro of NAV. That 44 cents has been falling for five years, and nothing yet obliges it to stop.

What the case is. A slowly rising NAV path (about 7% a year), resting almost wholly on strengths EXOR has demonstrated: Ferrari's compounding, a near-zero cost base, disposals at book value, and buybacks that add to NAV per share. The case carries a low risk of permanent loss. At an unchanged discount, it pays about 8% a year.
What the case is not, yet. A re-rating case. A re-rating needs a strength EXOR has not demonstrated: closing a family-controlled discount. EXOR's own buybacks have not closed it, its recurring income cannot fund a large enough flow of buybacks, and the cash that could do so is also wanted for a new stake.

Why EXOR is worth watching closely. Few stocks set out their branching point so clearly. The cash is half the value of the outside holders' shares; management's options and the family's need for liquidity both favour a tender; and the decision has a date. The right question in late March 2027 is not "was there a buyback?" but "how much cash reaches outside holders, relative to the €6.3bn of shares they own?"

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 56, set by the Rater. A mild net positive external balance (53) and a funded but undated internal programme (60) reach profits only as a clean EPS growth of about 6% to 8% a year (C, 55) from a 2027 trough, partly from buybacks and cyclical dividends, and as NAV growth below EXOR's past; the forces are real but neither large nor sure in their effect on profits, so a mild net positive in the high 50s, close to the memo's C.

Foundations' Robustness: 60, set by the Rater. Quality (57) rests on one top-decile franchise, a near debt-free A- balance sheet and a near-zero cost base that make permanent loss unlikely, offset by narrowing industrial moats, ordinary returns on new stakes and family control; the delivery record (52) of always-met conservative limits but a missed NAV-versus-index goal neither lifts nor sinks it, so the level's good unit-level moats with a strong balance sheet but no group mechanism, about 60.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 33, set by the Rater. The best fit is the memo's 'Major CfC Clearing in MQ non-cyclical or better business on Q1 multiple', and the Q1 multiple is present on price to NAV, but the setup's mechanism, the causes for concern clearing, is absent today (Stellantis still deteriorating, idle cash undecided, NAV still trailing the index, family control unchanged), and the portfolio still carries cyclical holdings, so current problems contradict the mechanism: a weak fit, a little above the level's 25.

Case Riskiness: 46, set by the Rater. Over topic 9 (45): a simple, trackable case with no balance-sheet or refinancing risk and a low risk of permanent loss, but an equity outcome much less predictable than its operating lines, carried by Ferrari's premium multiple, a discount that widens in every drawdown and one board decision, with a cone tilted down; the level's simple case with an unpredictable equity outcome, just below 50.

The ranges of outcome, sensitivity grid, income-mix bars and fair-multiple ladder restate the memo's own figures. Default charts and tables are FactSet and Viewforth dashboard outputs, with their notes beside each. The model's total-return horizons end on fixed dates after the last reported period.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. The percentile ("66th percentile") is the share of the stocks scored on that item that this stock beats. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
